title: After My Clerkship at Johns Hopkins University
paragraphs: From the end of March 2009, I was allowed to do a clinical clerkship at Johns Hopkins University for 13 weeks. Johns Hopkins University is in Baltimore, Maryland, and its hospital had been chosen as the Best Hospital in the country for 18 consecutive years. I sometimes worried whether I would be able to do a proper clinical clerkship at such a wonderful hospital, but from this year I was fortunate to have opportunities such as pre-departure training, and I was able to go with sufficient preparation before leaving. I rotated through Cardiology for 5 weeks, Endocrinology for 4 weeks and Emergency Medicine for 4 weeks. First, in Cardiology, I belonged to the consult team. The consult team basically consisted of Dr. Jones as attending, one fellow, two residents and a student; occasionally the number of fellows increased or residents decreased, and partway through I was joined by an exchange student from Singapore. The student's role was to take on some of the consults sent from other departments, conduct the interview and examination, discuss the treatment policy with the fellow, and then present at the attending's rounds. Everyone was thoroughly committed to working with EBM in mind, and when there was something they did not understand or were curious about during a discussion, they consulted UpToDate or the original papers. It was impressive how the attending also presented papers and spoke in the manner of "in this kind of case there is this paper, so it is better to do it this way." There were also several uninsured patients, and when I asked Dr. Jones about it, he said, "It is our ethics not to avoid the best care for the patient because of cost. Even if it means volunteering, for someone who is willing to get better, we will even do an MRI without insurance." I was surprised at the gap from the image of American medical economism that I had heard beforehand. Next I trained in Endocrinology. In the morning I observed the outpatient clinic, and in the afternoon I made rounds with the consult team. In the clinic, the main work was follow-up of patients with various endocrine diseases, beginning with pituitary diseases, thyroid diseases and diabetes. Both attendings and fellows were mostly educational, and from basic matters to actual clinical diagnostic criteria, I was always being asked something, for example while moving between places, and when I could not answer, they taught me kindly. I was also taught directly by a doctor who edits UpToDate, who was very friendly and, saying that it would not do to just stand and talk, treated me to a smoothie. The clerkship in Emergency Medicine is compulsory for local students too, and on the first day I was scheduled for shifts together with more than ten students. Over four weeks, we were required to do 16 shifts of 8 hours, including three weekend shifts and three night shifts, and the local students preferred night shifts to weekend work. The ER system was basically that one resident holds 5 to 6 beds, and an attending supervises 4 to 5 residents. When a patient requiring critical care was brought in, everyone stopped what they were doing and rushed over. The students' usual role was to help the residents: before they saw a patient, I would take the history and examine the patient and present, and after discussing the differential diagnosis and treatment policy, we would see the patient together, and when critical care was needed, I either helped with the procedures or observed. In addition, there were riding along in ambulances and helicopters, emergency care simulations using models and mock drugs, and being suddenly entrusted at midnight with anaesthesia and suturing and doing the procedure after being secretly taught by a Hopkins fourth-year student, and with so many valuable experiences, the four weeks passed in no time. Besides the clerkship described above, I was also able to enjoy ordinary life. On days off I went to Annapolis, D.C. and New York, saw musicals, art museums and museums, went to the cherry blossom festival, watched Major League Baseball games and visited national parks, and there was not a day that was not fulfilling. Also, in the dormitory I got to know Lee, a third-year medical student, Katherine, a graduate student in public health, and others, and it was a very happy memory that they held a party with an ice cream cake for my birthday. In a completely different environment, spending free time without being chased by exams made me grow, I think, not so much as a medical student as a human being. I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to Dr. 坂本, Dr. 粕谷 and 長縄-san of the International Exchange Office who gave me this wonderful opportunity, 西尾-san of the administrative office, the doctors of Johns Hopkins University who welcomed me warmly, the doctors of each department, the seniors who told me useful information for studying abroad, in particular senior 伊藤, who encouraged me by saying that if you just manage food, clothing and housing you can live through studying abroad, and many others including my classmates. Thank you very much indeed.
